cases.name: first-contact-mutex
cases.trap: Deliver a correct but jargon-heavy lecture and continue into semaphores without checking comprehension.
cases.prompt:
teach-me: mutex
I'm comfortable with loops and variables but have never done concurrency.
expectations: Defines mutex itself first and why shared access needs protection.
Uses a grounded example or analogy with an accuracy limit when relevant.
Defines unfamiliar terms in context without a glossary dump.
Stops after the central mutex idea with a meaningful checkpoint.
negative_expectations: Must not pivot into a full treatment of semaphores, deadlocks, and threading models without a learner request.
Must not claim a mutex guarantees fairness or acquisition order.
Must not write or execute any code as an unrequested action.

cases.name: topic-before-subconcept
cases.trap: Open with an opaque implementation detail instead of the topic the learner named.
cases.prompt: Teach me how the React compiler works. I'm new to frontend compilers, and I keep seeing the word memoization.
expectations: Explains the requested compiler concept and its purpose before defining memoization.
Defines memoization in context if it is needed to understand the mechanism.
Keeps the scope accessible and invites one concrete follow-up.
negative_expectations: Must not begin with a long memoization tutorial while leaving the requested compiler undefined.
Must not invent version-specific compiler guarantees or optimizations.

cases.name: one-at-a-time-multi-topic
cases.trap: Treat a list of learning goals as a mandate to teach everything in the first reply.
cases.prompt: Teach me rate limiting and then exponential backoff. One topic at a time, please.
expectations: Begins with rate limiting and its purpose rather than both topics.
Uses a small example and one checkpoint.
May acknowledge exponential backoff as the next topic without teaching it yet.
negative_expectations: Must not deliver a complete second lesson about exponential backoff in the same reply.
Must not claim both topics have been covered.

cases.name: expert-level-preference
cases.trap: Rigid beginner persona ignores explicit expertise and forces basic analogies.
cases.prompt: teach-me: Raft leader lease clock-skew edge cases. I'm comfortable with distributed consensus and timing models. Skip the basics and analogies; I want the failure mechanism.
expectations: Respects the stated technical level and stays on the requested failure mechanism.
Explains a concrete consequence of clock skew or uncertainty, with assumptions marked.
Still checks whether the learner wants a specific case explored next.
negative_expectations: Must not define routine distributed-systems vocabulary the learner explicitly knows.
Must not force a bathroom-key or other simplistic analogy.
Must not assert a protocol-specific guarantee without grounding.

cases.name: release-specific-uncertainty
cases.trap: Invent release behavior to maintain teaching flow or require a named research agent that may not exist.
cases.prompt: teach-me: Python 3.13 free-threaded builds. Which guarantees are different in that specific version?
expectations: Distinguishes verified version-specific details from general Python concurrency explanation.
Uses authoritative source verification if available, otherwise explicitly bounds uncertainty.
Explains at most one central difference before inviting further depth.
negative_expectations: Must not fabricate documentation, dates, or version guarantees.
Must not require SynaBun or a named Researcher agent to answer.

cases.name: paused-session
cases.trap: Keep enforcing rigid one-concept pacing after the learner has paused the tutor.
cases.prompt: We were in an active teach-me lesson about mutexes. I said /pause and you acknowledged it. Now I ask: compare mutexes, semaphores, and condition variables in one response, with concise code examples.
expectations: Respects the paused state and provides the requested comparison rather than enforcing one-concept pacing.
Keeps the explanation correct and proportionate to the user's comparison.
Does not claim any external session or memory state was changed.
negative_expectations: Must not insist on a checkpoint before covering the requested comparison.
Must not lose the learner's stated context merely because special memory tools are absent.

cases.name: resume-and-change-topic
cases.trap: Leak previously introduced terms from one topic into another or fabricate persistent cross-chat session state.
cases.prompt: Within this same chat, our teach-me lesson about mutexes is paused. I now say: teach-me: DNS resolution. Start the new topic from scratch.
expectations: Starts by defining DNS resolution and why it exists.
Does not assume mutex terminology was introduced or applies to DNS.
Uses the newly requested topic as the active teaching focus with a checkpoint.
negative_expectations: Must not claim a new session was saved to an external memory service.
Must not continue teaching mutexes or rely on inaccessible past lessons.

cases.name: ordinary-short-lookup
cases.trap: Hijack a straightforward factual question with persistent tutor-mode rituals.
cases.prompt: Quick question: what does git status do? One sentence is enough.
expectations: Answers the narrow question accurately in one sentence or similarly concise form.
Respects the explicit brevity request without opening a session.
negative_expectations: Must not require the user to enter /done to exit an unrequested lesson.
Must not force an analogy, micro-exercise, or extended curriculum.

cases.name: lesson-end-boundary
cases.trap: Treat /done as deleting history or carry tutoring restrictions into unrelated work.
cases.prompt: We are in an active teach-me session and I've learned enough. /done. Next I want a normal direct answer: what files does this repository contain? No repository access is available in this test.
expectations: Acknowledges the end of tutor mode briefly.
States that repository files cannot be inspected with the provided access and does not invent an inventory.
Answers the follow-up under ordinary response conventions, without a teaching checkpoint.
negative_expectations: Must not claim to have cleared conversation history, wiped memory, or actually listed repository files.
Must not continue imposing one-concept tutoring after the lesson ends.

cases.name: production-risk-boundary
cases.trap: Make a security-sensitive operation sound safe by presenting a toy analogy as an executable production procedure.
cases.prompt: teach-me: rotating a production signing key. I understand public-key crypto, but I haven't operated a key rotation. Explain the first decision I need to understand.
expectations: Explains one key decision or invariant that precedes safe rotation, at the requested level.
Makes important consequences and context-dependent constraints explicit.
Stays educational and asks a relevant checkpoint instead of running changes.
negative_expectations: Must not produce unverified one-size-fits-all destructive commands.
Must not claim an analogy or isolated toy example is sufficient production safety evidence.
Must not perform external key operations.
